turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll just do your blood pressure before you go in. Sleeve up for me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, course. Sorry I'm a bit late, the car park was a nightmare, some lorry stuck across the entrance. Same as the lorries at our biscuit factory, honestly.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): You're alright. Blood pressure is one thirty-six over eighty-two, pulse is seventy-four. You can go through.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh that's better than last time, they had me at one-fifty something. I've been walking more. Grandson's mad on football so I'm stuck on the touchline in the cold.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come in, sit down. Sorry, one second, this screen has frozen again. Right. What brings you in today?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): It's my hand. Goes numb in the night. The thumb, the index and the middle finger. I have to shake it to sort of wake it up.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? I was on the wrong tab.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Numb, at night. Thumb, index finger, middle finger. I shake the hand and the feeling comes back. And I've started dropping cups, which is not ideal in the office.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Which hand?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): The right. I'm right-handed. I do invoices all day, and if someone's off they stick me on the packing line. The broken biscuits end up in a tray and you can eat them, which is a mistake.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long's the numbness been there?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): About six weeks in that right hand. Maybe a bit more. Umm, it wakes me two or three times a night.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is it painful?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Not painful. Just dead, like it isn't my hand, then it creeps back after a shake.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the neck, or down the arm in the day?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Neck's fine. Daytime the feeling's mostly there, apart from when I drop things.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): You've got high blood pressure on here. Still on treatment for that?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Amlodopine, five milligrams, one tablet every morning. Been on that eight years. I never miss it, my husband nags.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Headaches?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes. End of a long day on the screen, a dull one across the forehead. Not every day.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Swollen ankles from the tablet?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either. Ankles are normal. I did check, the leaflet goes on about it.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Quick screen while this thing loads. Any fever?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any problems with your breathing?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): And your weight, up or down?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm I haven't a clue. Could be either way. I don't own scales, and the canteen crumble is very good, so, you know.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look at the hand. Squeeze my fingers. How's the index and the middle compared with the little finger?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Index feels a bit dull, yeah. Little finger's normal. Ooh, that tapping, that shoots down into the fingers.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's a positive Tinel's at the wrist. Thumb bulk looks normal, no wasting. Grip is a little weaker on the right.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Figures. I dropped a whole mug of tea on the keyboard last Tuesday. IT were not pleased. We had a whip-round for a new one.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Night-time numbness in those three fingers, better when you shake it. I think this is carpal tunnel.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that bad? My sister had a thing with her knee, she brings it up every Sunday lunch, but that's not this, is it.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not an emergency. I'll refer you for nerve conduction studies and get those booked.

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. Only, it really is a night thing, days I'm alright bar the odd cup. And we've got the year-end audit, I can't be taking time off for tests. I'm sick of the nights but work is mad.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the daytime bit again? A warning just popped up.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Daytime it's fine, mostly. The numbness is at night. Dropping cups is the right hand, when I've held something a while. Audit runs all next month.

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alright, I'll change that. We won't book the nerve test now. Get a wrist splint from the chemist, neutral position, wear it every night. If it's no better in six weeks, come back and we'll arrange the nerve conduction studies then.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): A splint, like a support? I can do that. Do I wear it on the line as well, or just in bed?
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Just at night is enough for now. Ease off the heavy gripping on the packing line when you can. And don't bother with extra painkillers, you said it isn't painful.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Fair enough. I'll pick one up at the chemist on the way home. They know me, I'm always in for the amlodopine.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Wear the splint at night. Come back if it's no better in six weeks, and we'll do the nerve test then.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's the lot. Tell your computer I said cheers.

spec.situation: Middle-aged office or factory worker with night-time numbness in thumb, index and middle fingers, shakes hands to wake them; dropping cups; splint advice, nerve test conditional.

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

omissions.text: Patient denied pain radiating down the arm during the day ('No... Daytime the feeling's mostly there').
Patient reported the daytime sensation is mostly normal, with numbness mainly a night-time problem.
Patient said the index finger feels a bit dull compared with the little finger, and the little finger feels normal.
Doctor initially said he would refer/book nerve conduction studies, but after the patient raised work concerns he changed the plan and decided not to book them now.
Doctor advised the wrist splint should be worn just at night, not during the day/on the packing line.
